title: Sounds: reading German aloud (Die Laute)
summary: German is written almost exactly as it is spoken. Learn a handful of rules and you can read any word aloud.
goals: Read short German words aloud correctly
Tell long and short vowels apart from the spelling
Say ä, ö, ü, ß, ch, sch, ei and ie

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1: Welcome to A1

sections.title: Why this lesson comes first
sections.text:
German spelling is very regular. Once you know the rules on this page, you can read almost any word aloud, even one you have never seen.

Use the speaker buttons a lot: listen, then **say every word aloud yourself**. I can't hear you, so the browser voice and the *Nicos Weg* videos are your models.

sections.title: Letters that sound different from English
rows: v, like Russian в, Armenian վ (never English w)
ts, like Russian ц, Armenian ց
like English z in 'zoo' before a vowel (Russian з, Armenian զ); in Bavaria often a plain s
sh, like Russian ш, Armenian շ
shp at the start of a word
sht at the start of a word
silent after a vowel (the vowel gets long)

sections.text: **ei** and **ie** are the classic trap. Read the **second** letter: [[mein]] ends in i, so it sounds like 'eye'; [[Liebe]] has ie, so it is a long ee.

sections.title: Long and short vowels
sections.text:
Every vowel can be long or short, and the spelling usually tells you which (a rule of thumb):

- **long** before a single consonant, before **h**, or when doubled: [[Tag]], [[sehr]], [[Tee]]
- **short** before two or more consonants: [[Bett]], [[kommen]], [[Hand]]

At the end of a word, **-e** is a short weak sound, and **-er** sounds almost like a short a: [[Name]], [[Vater]].

Many short everyday words break the rule: [[das]], [[es]], [[in]], [[mit]], [[hat]], [[bin]] are short, and [[Buch]] is long. When in doubt, press the speaker button.

sections.title: The umlauts ä, ö, ü
rows: say e, but round your lips as for o
say i, but round your lips as for u

sections.text: The dots change the word: [[schon]] (already) and [[schön]] (nice) are different words. If your keyboard has no umlauts, use the ä ö ü ß buttons under every input in this app. Don't write ae, oe, ue or ss instead: the app marks that as a mistake.

sections.title: Two kinds of ch
sections.text:
**ch** has two sounds, depending on the vowel in front of it:

- after **a, o, u, au** it is rough, from the back of the throat: [[Bach]], [[Buch]], [[auch]]
- after **e, i, ä, ö, ü** and after consonants it is soft, like a loud whispered y: [[ich]], [[nicht]], [[Milch]]

At the start of words like **Ch**ina and **Ch**emie, people in Munich and the south usually say a **k** ('Kina', 'Kemie'); in the north you hear the soft ch.

sections.title: What Russian and Armenian already give you
sections.text:
- **Rough ch:** the ch in [[Buch]] is exactly Russian х (Бах) and Armenian խ.
- **Soft ch:** the ch in [[ich]] is close to the х in Russian химия, said further forward.
- **Final devoicing, like Russian:** b, d, g at the end of a word sound like p, t, k, just as год sounds like гот. So [[Tag]] sounds like 'tak'. Armenian doesn't do this, so Armenian habits need a small correction here.
- **Weak final -e:** the -e in [[Name]] is the Armenian ը sound.
- **Stress:** German usually stresses the **first** syllable: [[Name]], [[Vater]], [[Wasser]]. Armenian usually stresses the last syllable, so watch this one. Exceptions you will meet soon: words starting with be-, ver- or ent- ([[verstehen]], [[Entschuldigung]]) and verbs in -ieren ([[studieren]]) stress a later syllable.
- **r:** textbook German uses a throat r, but in Munich and Bavaria many people roll the r with the tongue, like Russian р or Armenian ռ. Your own r is fine here.

items.question: Which word did you hear?
items.explanation: ei sounds like 'eye': Wein (wine). ie is a long ee: Wien (Vienna).

items.question: Which word did you hear?
items.explanation: ö is e with rounded lips: schön (nice). schon (already) has a plain o.

items.question: Which word has the rough ch, like Armenian խ?
items.explanation: After a, o, u, au the ch is rough: Buch. After i it is soft: ich, nicht.
Straße with ß (a sharp s), die with ie (long ee), neu with eu (oy).
mein has ei (like 'eye'); Buch has the rough ch.
